items.title: The NIST Toolkit for US and International Security
items.summary: The National Institute of Standards and Technology produces some of the world's most widely used cybersecurity frameworks. This lesson explains what NIST publishes, why organisations use its frameworks, and how its products differ from ISO and other standards.
objectives: List the NIST publications most relevant to enterprise GRC professionals
Explain the difference between a framework, a standard and a guideline
Describe the relationship between NIST CSF, NIST RMF, SP 800-53 and NIST SP 800-171
Explain why an organisation outside the US uses NIST frameworks

sections.heading: What NIST is and what it publishes
sections.body: The National Institute of Standards and Technology is part of the US Department of Commerce. It is a standards body - it publishes technical standards, guidelines, best practice and frameworks. NIST does not regulate; it informs.
bullets: NIST produces standards (for example FIPS for cryptographic modules)
NIST produces guidelines (for example SP 800-53 for security controls)
NIST produces frameworks (for example the Cybersecurity Framework)
NIST publications are voluntary but widely adopted

sections.heading: Why NIST matters outside the US
sections.body: Although NIST is a US federal agency, its publications are used worldwide. The reasons include:
bullets: NIST publications are authoritative and well documented
Many international standards are influenced by NIST
US government procurement requires NIST compliance
The frameworks are practical and risk-based

sections.heading: The Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)
sections.body: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is the most widely known NIST product. It provides a common language for describing cybersecurity risk.
bullets: Five functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
CSF 2.0 added three more functions
Frameworks are not prescriptive - they are descriptions
Organisations map their controls to the functions

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-53: Security and Privacy Controls
sections.body: NIST Special Publication 800-53 provides a catalogue of security and privacy controls for information systems.
bullets: Over 100 security controls in the catalogue
Controls are grouped by type: access control, audit, encryption, and more
Baselines are levels of control - Low, Moderate, High
The catalogue is the basis of many international control schemes

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-171: Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information
sections.body: SP 800-171 is the control set used when organisations handle Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI).
bullets: 64 security requirements for CUI
Used by defence contractors
Most widely used third-party security assessment
Controls cover access control, audit, configuration, and more

practicalExercise.title: Map NIST CSF to ISO 27001
practicalExercise.brief: Write a table mapping 5 NIST CSF 2.0 functions to the ISO 27001 clauses most relevant to each.
steps: For each function, identify relevant ISO 27001 clauses
Document the mapping in a table
evaluationCriteria: Mapping demonstrates understanding of both frameworks

items.title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
items.summary: CSF 2.0 is the most widely used cybersecurity framework in the world. This lesson covers all six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
objectives: List the six functions of CSF 2.0 and explain what each does
Explain organisational profiles, tiers and gaps in CSF context
Apply CSF 2.0 to a real organisational scenario
Explain the difference between CSF and NIST SP 800-53

sections.heading: What CSF 2.0 is
sections.body: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 provides a common language for describing cybersecurity risk. It is not a standard - it is a description of what good looks like.
bullets: Used by organisations of all sizes worldwide
Flexible: no mandatory controls
Built around six functions
Used for board reporting, strategy and compliance

sections.heading: GOV: Governance
sections.body: The Govern function provides the governance framework for the cybersecurity programme.
bullets: Framework policy: written statement of cybersecurity intent
Organisational context: the environment the organisation operates in
Roles and responsibilities: who does what
Cyber risk management: how risk is managed at board level
Drivers: legal, regulatory, market and risk

sections.heading: ID: Identify
sections.body: The Identify function focuses on understanding the organisation's assets and the risks to them.
bullets: Asset management: what do you own?
Business environment: what is the organisation?
Governance: who makes decisions?
Risk assessment: what could go wrong?
Risk management strategy: what is the appetite?

sections.heading: PR: Protect
sections.body: The Protect function describes the safeguards that reduce or remove risks to operations.
bullets: Awareness and training: people are the first line of defence
Access control: who gets in?
Data security: protecting information
Information protection procedures: how data is handled
Maintenance: keeping systems running
Protective technology: how technology defends

sections.heading: DE: Detect
sections.body: The Detect function describes how the organisation identifies cybersecurity events.
bullets: Anomalies and events: what might hint at an incident?
Detection processes: how are incidents found?
Continuous monitoring: what are you looking for?

sections.heading: RS: Respond
sections.body: The Respond function describes what the organisation does when an incident occurs.
bullets: Response planning: what happens when?
Communications: who tells whom?
Analysis: what has happened?
Mitigation: what are you doing about it?
Improvements: what will you do differently?

sections.heading: RC: Recover
sections.body: The Recover function describes the organisation's ability to restore capabilities or services impaired during an incident.
bullets: Recovery planning: how will you get back to normal?
Communications: who tells whom during recovery?
Improvements: what will you do differently?

sections.heading: Profiles, tiers and gaps
sections.body: CSF 2.0 introduces three concepts that make it practical:
bullets: Profiles: a snapshot of your current state and your target state
Tiers: how mature is your programme? (0-4)
Gaps: what is missing between where you are and where you want to be?

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Write a short profile for a fictional company: current state, target state, and the top three gaps between them.
bullets: Current state: what do you do today?
Target state: what do you want to achieve?
Gaps: what do you need to do to get there?

practicalExercise.title: CSF 2.0 Profile for a fictional company
practicalExercise.brief: Write a profile for a fictional company with 500 employees and internet banking operations.
steps: List the top three gaps between them
